title: Global sections as invariants
statement:
Keep the notation of [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence]. Let $U_0\subseteq C_0$ be a
nonempty open subscheme, $U=U_0\times_{\Fq}k$ its base change and $\pi_1(U)$
its geometric fundamental group; restriction gives the Weil group $W(U_0)$
of [def-wf-weil-group]
with geometric subgroup $\pi_1(U)$. For a subgroup $I$ write
$V^{I}=\{v\in V:gv=v\text{ for all }g\in I\}$ for the invariants of
[def-real-weil-representation-operations], and let
$H^0$ denote ordinary etale global
sections. Then

$$
H^0\bigl(U,\mathcal F|_{U}\bigr)=V^{\pi_1(U)},
$$

compatibly with the residual action of $F=\rho(\gamma)$ on both sides, where
$\rho$ is the Weil fundamental representation of
[def-wf-fundamental-representation].

proof.text: Hypotheses on the geometric curve. By [d-real-setup], $C_0\to\operatorname{Spec}k_0$ is separated, smooth and of finite type, $C_0$ is nonempty of pure dimension one [def-weil-pure-dimension], and $C=C_0\times_{k_0}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is connected. The base change $C\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is separated by [lem-weil-pbc-separated-base-change], of finite type by clause (2) of [lem-sfb-finite-type-composition-base-change], and smooth by clause (2) of [lem-pc-proper-base-change]. Dimension (topological Krull dimension): a chain of irreducible closed subsets of $C_0$ lies in an irreducible component containing its top member, so $\dim C_0=1$, and every affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq C_0$ has $\dim\le1$ (closures turn a chain in an open into a chain in $C_0$). By [lem-weil-pbc-dimension-preserved-field-extension] the opens $\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_{k_0}k)$, which cover $C$, also have $\dim\le1$; a scheme is $T_0$ and quasi-sober by [lem-sc-scheme-sober], so [lem-weil-pbc-dimension-bound-open-cover] gives $\dim C\le1$. Conversely take a component $Z$ of $C_0$ with generic point $\xi$ and an irreducible closed $Z'\subsetneq Z$ with generic point $z'$ [lem-sc-scheme-sober], and an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A\ni z'$. It contains $\xi$, since $z'\in\overline{\{\xi\}}$, and $\xi\notin Z'$; so $Z'\cap\operatorname{Spec}A\subsetneq Z\cap\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a chain of length one, $\dim\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_{k_0}k)\ge1$ by the same lemma, and its closure chain gives $\dim C\ge1$. Hence $C$ is a nonempty connected smooth curve of dimension one over the algebraically closed field $k$ in the sense of [def-sc-curves].

source.place: First sentence: 'on the connected U'; the standing curve C of the chapter is a smooth connected curve over k (reviewer FIX)

proof.text: By Step 1, clause 1 of [lem-sc-smooth-connected-curve-local-rings] makes $C$ Noetherian and integral. The smooth curve $C$ is normal by [lem-sc-smooth-normal]. Its nonempty open $U$ is therefore irreducible and connected: two nonempty opens of $U$ are nonempty opens of the irreducible space $C$, so intersect. Also $U$ is dense in $C$. Moreover $U_0$ is dense in $C_0$: by [lem-weil-pbc-base-change-image], applied to $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}k_0$ (surjective onto the one-point space) and $C_0\to\operatorname{Spec}k_0$, the projection $C\to C_0$ is surjective; $U$ is the preimage of $U_0$, so $C$, the image of $\overline U$, lies in $\overline{U_0}$. The open $U$ is Noetherian and separated, by restriction from $C$. The prime $\ell$ is invertible on $U$ since $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}(k)$. Thus the underlying lisse-sheaf equivalence may be applied on $U$, with the same geometric generic point and stalk $V$.

source.place: First sentence: 'on the connected U'; verify the hypotheses of the underlying fibre equivalence

proof.text: Put $\mathcal G=\mathcal F|_U$ and let $\mathbf1_U$ be the rank-one coefficient sheaf. A global section $s$ gives the sheaf morphism $m_s:\mathbf1_U\to\mathcal G$ defined by $a\mapsto a\,s|_T$ over each etale $T\to U$; conversely a coefficient-linear sheaf morphism $m$ gives $m_U(1)$. These constructions are inverse, since a local scalar multiplies the restriction of $1$, and this can be checked on a cover on which that scalar is constant. For adic coefficients use precisely [def-pod-lisse-l-adic-sheaves]: at $\mathcal O_E$ both sides are compatible families of these finite-level maps or sections; at $E$ both are rationalized, and at $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ morphisms and sections are taken over a common finite coefficient field and then extended. The same formulas respect transition maps and scalar extension. Hence ordinary adic global sections identify with $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf1_U,\mathcal G)$ in the category of underlying lisse sheaves, without requiring the morphism to preserve a Weil structure.

source.place: Second sentence: a global section is a morphism from the constant rank-one sheaf

proof.text: Apply clause 2 of [cor-galois-lisse-representations] to $U$, whose hypotheses were checked in Steps 1 and 2. The fibre functor is an equivalence and sends the unit sheaf to the trivial representation. Consequently it identifies $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf1_U,\mathcal G)$ with the $\pi_1(U)$-equivariant $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-linear maps $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\to V$. By [def-wf-fundamental-representation], the action on this fibre is exactly the restriction of the Weil fundamental representation to the geometric subgroup. It is the underlying geometric equivalence that is used here; imposing Weil-equivariance on these maps would incorrectly impose the additional equation $Fv=v$.

source.place: Second sentence: under the equivalence, morphisms are maps of geometric fundamental-group representations

proof.text: For such an equivariant map $f$, put $v=f(1)$. Since the source action is trivial, $gv=f(g1)=f(1)=v$ for every $g\in\pi_1(U)$, so $v$ lies in the invariant subspace of [def-real-weil-representation-operations]. Conversely, for an invariant vector $v$, the map $f_v(a)=av$ is linear and satisfies $g f_v(a)=a(gv)=av=f_v(a)$. The two maps are inverse since $f(a)=af(1)$, and preserve addition and scalars. Combining Steps 3 and 4 gives the asserted canonical identification $s\mapsto s_{\bar\eta}$ from $H^0(U,\mathcal G)$ to $V^{\pi_1(U)}$.

source.place: Third and fourth sentences: evaluation at 1 and its inverse

proof.text: Write $r:W(U_0)\to W(C_0)$ for restriction and $\sigma=\rho\circ r$. Clause 2 of [lem-wf-dense-open-pi1-surjective] applies by Steps 1 and 2 and lifts the fixed degree-one $\gamma\in W(C_0)$ to a degree-one $\widetilde\gamma\in W(U_0)$. By [lem-wf-weil-group-exact-sequence], $P=\pi_1(U)$ is the kernel of the degree map. Thus $\widetilde\gamma^{-1}g\widetilde\gamma\in P$ for $g\in P$. For $v\in V^P$ we have $g\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)v=\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)\sigma(\widetilde\gamma^{-1}g\widetilde\gamma)v=\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)v$; the same calculation for the inverse lift proves that $F=\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)=\rho(\gamma)$ acts invertibly on $V^P$. On sections the Weil action sends $m:\mathbf1_U\to\mathcal G$ to $\varphi\circ\Phi_U^*m$, identifying $\Phi_U^*\mathbf1_U=\mathbf1_U$. On the stalk, with the transport of [def-wf-fundamental-representation], this is $f\mapsto\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)\circ f$: pullback and transport fix the source unit $1$, and the target operator is the one defining $\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)$. Evaluation gives $(\sigma(\widetilde\gamma)\circ f)(1)=Ff(1)$, proving equivariance. Another lift differs by an element of $P$, which acts trivially on the invariants, so this is the residual action.

source.place: Last two sentences: normality, preservation of invariants, and residual Frobenius equivariance
